english: But men of God carrying in them a holy spirit and becoming prophets, being inspired and made wise by God, became God-taught, and holy, and righteous.
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: Prophets are men who carry a holy spirit (pneuma hagion) and are inspired by God; the Greek uses 'pneuma hagion' with the article absent.
limits: Shows the Spirit as the agent of prophetic inspiration beside the Word and Wisdom, but Theophilus does not call the Spirit a person or a divine agent distinct from God here; the Greek is 'a holy spirit' without an identifying article in the first clause. Dods' chapter heading 'The Prophets Inspired by the Holy Ghost' is the ANF editor's, not Theophilus's.

english: But what else is this voice but the Word of God, who is also His Son? Not as the poets and writers of myths talk of the sons of gods begotten from intercourse [with women], but as truth ex
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: The 'voice' heard by Adam in Paradise is the Word of God, 'who is also His Son' (hos estin kai huios autou); the Greek word is 'huios' (the only explicit 'Son' in Books II-III found in the English).
limits: Only explicit use of 'Son' for the Word found in the English text of Books I-III; Theophilus contrasts it with the mythological 'sons of gods' by generation from intercourse, and calls the Word 'endiathetos' in the next clause. Subordinationist readers cite the 'and also His Son' clause; Trinitarian defenders read it with the Word as eternal (endiathetos). Greek read from scan; the same paragraph goes on (p. 118-120) to the 'counsellor' phrase, not read here (outside my range).

greek: Ἐκβληθεὶς δὲ Ἀδὰμ ἐκ τοῦ παραδείσου οὕτως ἔγνω Εὔαν τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, ἣν ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησεν αὐτῷ εἰς γυναῖκα ἐκ τῆς πλευρᾶς αὐτοῦ. Καὶ τοῦτο δὲ οὐχ ὡς μὴ δυνάμενος κατ’ ἰδίαν πλάσαι τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ προηπίστατο ὁ θεὸς ὅτι ἥμελλον οἱ ἄνθρωποι πληθὺν θεῶν ὀνομάζειν. Προγνώστης οὖν ὢν καὶ εἰδὼς ὅτι ἡ πλάνη ἤμελλεν διὰ τοῦ ὄφεως ὀνομάζειν πληθὺν θεῶν τῶν οὐκ ὄντων (ἑνὸς γὰρ ὄντος θεοῦ, ἔκτοτε ἤδη ἐμελέτα ἡ πλάνη πληθύνειν θεῶν ὑποσπείρειν καὶ λέγειν

english: for there being but one God, even then error was striving to disseminate a multitude of gods
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: God foresaw that men would name many gods; error began to spread many gods as soon as there was one God (ἑνὸς γὰρ ὄντος θεοῦ).
limits: Strict monotheist wording ('there being but one God') that Unitarians and Muslim polemicists can cite as Theophilus's own doctrine of one God; no Son or Spirit appears in the passage. Trinitarian defenders reply that 'one God' names the Father-Logos-Spirit unity and that the passage opposes idols, not Christ. Greek read from scan (ἥμελλον/ἤμελλεν spelling as printed).

what_it_says: The Holy Spirit (to pneuma to hagion) teaches all these genealogical and historical things through Moses and the prophets; the Greek is the phrase 'pneuma hagion' with the article.
limits: The phrase 'to pneuma to hagion' is a personal-sounding agent who teaches and speaks through Moses; it is the clearest 'Holy Spirit' wording so far in Book II. Διὸ δείκνυται πάντας τοὺς λοιποὺς πεπλανῆσθαι, μόνους δὲ Χριστιανοὺς τὴν ἀλήθειαν κεχωρηκέναι, οἵτινες ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου διδασκόμεθα, τοῦ λαλήσαντος ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις προφήταις καὶ τὰ πάντα προκαταγγελόντος.

english: and that we Christians alone have possessed the truth, inasmuch as we are taught by the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the holy prophets, and foretold all things.
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight

what_it_says: Christians alone have the truth because they are taught by the Holy Spirit (hypo pneumatos hagiou), who spoke in the holy prophets and foretold all things.
limits: The Spirit (pneuma hagion) is the teacher of Christians and the speaker in the prophets; this is a clear 'Holy Spirit' statement. The same Greek also says 'Christians' (Χριστιανοὺς) as the self-designation of the readers. Limits: no statement that the Spirit is God, consubstantial or a person; the Dods chapter heading 'Holy Ghost' is editorial, not Theophilus's. Greek line-break between 'ἀλήθειαν' and 'κεχωρηκέναι' resolved from a 300 dpi crop.

greek: Ὁ μὲν οὖν θεῖος νόμος οὐ μόνον κωλύει τὸ εἰδώλοις προσκυνεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς στοιχείοις, ἡλίῳ σελήνῃ ἢ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἄστροις, ἀλλ’ οὔτε τῷ οὐρανῷ οὔτε γῇ οὔτε θαλάσσῃ ἢ πηγαῖς ἢ ποταμοῖς θρησκεύειν. ἀλλ’ ἢ μόνῳ τῷ ὄντως θεῷ καὶ ποιητῇ τῶν ὅλων χρὴ λατρεύειν ἐν ὁσιότητι καρδίας καὶ εἰλικρινεῖ γνώμῃ.

english: The divine law, then, not only forbids the worshipping of idols, but also of the heavenly bodies, the sun, the moon, or the other stars; yea, not heaven, nor earth, nor the sea, nor fountains, nor rivers, must be worshipped, but we must serve in holiness of heart and sincerity of purpose only the living and true God, who also is Maker of the universe.
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: Worship is due only to 'the truly existing God, Maker of the universe' (monō tō ontōs theō kai poiētē tōn holōn); the divine law forbids worship of idols, stars, earth, sea and rivers.
limits: Exclusive worship of 'the one truly existing God' is the Unitarian and Muslim-facing point. Limits: the Greek says 'tō ontōs theō' (the truly existing God); Dods' 'living and true God' adds 'living', which is not in the Greek as read. No Son, Word or Spirit is named in the sentence.

greek: Ἄνθρωποι θνητοὶ καὶ σάρκινοι, οὐδὲν ὄντες, πῶς ταχέως ὑψοῦσθε, βίου τέλος οὐκ ἐσορῶντες; Οὐ τρέμετ’, οὐδὲ φοβεῖσθε θεόν, τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ὑμῶν, ὕψιστον γνώστην, πανεπόπτην, μάρτυρα πάντων, Πάντοτροφον κτίστην, ὅστις γλυκὺ πνεῦμ’ ἐν ἁπασι, Κάτθετο, χήγητῆρα βροτῶν πάντων ἐποίησεν· Εἷς Θεός, ὃς μόνος ἄρχει, ὑπερμεγέθης, ἀγέννητος, Παντοκράτωρ, ἀόρατος, ὁρῶν μόνος αὐτὸς ἅπαντα. Αὐτὸς δ’ οὐ βλέπεται θνητῆς ὑπὸ σαρκὸς ἁπάσης.

english: Your Overseer, the Knower, Seer of all, / Who ever keeps those whom His hand first made, / Puts His sweet Spirit into all His works, / And gives Him for a guide to mortal men. / There is one only uncreated God, / Who reigns alone, all-powerful, very great, / From whom is nothing hid.
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: Quotes the Sibyl: God is the one who 'puts His sweet Spirit (gluku pneum' en hapasi) into all His works', and 'Eis Theos' (one God) who alone rules, uncreated, invisible.
limits: Gives a 'Spirit' of God as creative breath in all works, which is a pneuma-as-power usage (not a named person); and a strict 'Eis Theos' monotheism taken from a non-Christian poem (Sibylline oracle), which Theophilus treats as prophecy. Limits: the Sibyl is a Greek oracle collection with Jewish influence, quoted by Theophilus; Dods prints the oracle as verse. From the scan: 'Κάτθετο' spelling as printed; line numbers 1-10 of the apparatus were ignored.

translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight
edition: Otto 1861 (Corpus Apologetarum VIII, Ienae: F. Mauke); Google scan on archive.org (archive.org metadata wrongly gives 1851; title page reads MDCCCLXI)
what_it_says: Orpheus, who rejected his 365 gods, is said to have taught 'in his Diathekai' that there is 'one God' (hena einai theon).
limits: Theophilus's 'one God' here is Orpheus's teaching, not a Christian formula, so it is evidence that monotheism was a pagan philosophical claim in his argument; the phrase 'en tais Diathekais autou' (his 'Diathekai', i.e. Orpheus's precepts) is not Scripture. Limits: the first clause of the sentence (before 'ἀθετεῖ') is on the preceding line and was not read on this scan; English exact from Dods.

Of this divine law, then, Moses, who also was God's servant, was made the minister both to all the world, and chiefly to the Hebrews
translator: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), New Advent revision by Kevin Knight

what_it_says: Gives the law of God as the divine law (theios nomos) quoted from Exodus 23:6-8 (the 'Exod. 23' law), and calls Moses 'God's servant' (therapon tou theou) and 'minister' (diakonos) of that law.
limits: Shows the 'law' and the servant-minister vocabulary (therapon, diakonos) that opponents apply to the Word as servant/minister; here the titles belong to Moses, not to the Word. Theophilus's opening confession 'God exists, but He is one' (Dods 3.9) is on Otto p. 212 (PDF 327), which is too smeared to read in this scan, so its Greek is not verified. Dods' 'Now we also confess that God exists, but that He is one...' is therefore unverified in Greek.

what_it_says: The 'Jesus' of this chronology is Joshua son of Nave (Iēsous huios Nauē), successor of Moses, not Jesus Christ.
limits: Negative result for 'Jesus': the only occurrence of 'Jesus' (Iesous) in the work's text read here names Joshua son of Nave; the Dods English 'sun of Nun' is a typo for 'son'; the Greek reads 'huios Nauē'. Use this to answer anyone who cites 'Jesus' in Theophilus as Christ. The English text of Books I-III has only these two occurrences of 'Jesus', both naming Joshua.

what_it_says: The Greeks neglected and even blasphemed 'the glory of the incorruptible and only God' (tou aphthartou kai monou theou).
limits: 'Only God' (monos theos) is the strongest monotheist phrase in Book III and the one Unitarians cite for exclusive divinity of the Father; Theophilus gives 'only God' as the object of Christian reverence without naming a second person. Trinitarian reply: 'monos' here contrasts God with the idols, not with the Word. Greek read from 200 dpi crops (lines 'ἐπελάθοντο ἀλλὰ καὶ κατελάλησαν' confirmed).
